notes.front: What is structured data?
notes.back: Highly organised, well-defined information, typically held in tables with clear relationships between rows and columns.
notes.explanation: The study guide places it at the organised end of three types of data, with unstructured data at the other end.
notes.example: Like a train timetable: every row is a service, every column a station, and each cell holds a time.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Types of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is unstructured data?
notes.back: Information with no predefined data model or organisation, such as text documents and video files.
notes.explanation: The study guide notes that analysing it historically required machine learning.
notes.example: Like a shoebox of handwritten letters and holiday videos: a support team’s recorded phone calls and free-text emails.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Types of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is semi-structured data?
notes.back: Data that lacks a formal database structure but contains tags that label its parts.
notes.explanation: It falls between the other two types; the study guide spells it ‘semistructured’.
notes.example: Like a filing card with printed labels (‘Name:’, ‘Order:’) but no fixed form: a web shop’s order records where each entry names its own fields.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Types of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is first-party data?
notes.back: Proprietary customer data that a business collects directly, through its own transactions and digital interactions with its audience.
notes.explanation: The ‘party’ refers to who collected it: here the business itself, from its own customers.
notes.example: Like a corner shop’s own ledger of what regulars buy: a streaming service’s record of what each subscriber watches on its app.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Types of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is second-party data?
notes.back: Data owned by another organisation, such as a partner, that a company uses to augment its own internal data.
notes.explanation: It is someone else’s data, but it comes from an organisation the company has a relationship with, such as a partner.
notes.example: Like borrowing a neighbour’s notes on local plumbers: a cinema chain receives a partner restaurant’s booking data to enrich its own customer list.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Types of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is third-party data?
notes.back: External data collected by organisations that have no direct relationship with the customers concerned.
notes.explanation: The collector stands outside both the business and its partners, which is what makes it the third party.
notes.example: Like a national census table bought from a statistics publisher: a car dealer buys regional income figures from a data broker.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Types of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a database?
notes.back: An organised collection of data stored in tables and accessed electronically from a computer system.
notes.explanation: The study guide lists it first of three ways to store data, before the data warehouse and the data lake.
notes.example: Like a card index kept on a computer: a dental practice’s list of patients and appointments that its booking app reads and updates.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data storage”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a data warehouse?
notes.back: An enterprise system for analysing and reporting on structured and semi-structured data drawn from multiple sources.
notes.explanation: The study guide stresses two things: analysis and reporting, and data drawn from multiple sources.
notes.example: Like a head office that gathers every branch’s sales ledgers to compile the annual report: a retail group’s central store of sales data from all its regions.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data storage”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a data lake?
notes.back: A repository that can ingest, store, explore, process and analyse any type or volume of raw data, whatever its source.
notes.explanation: The words ‘any type’ and ‘raw’ set it apart from the data warehouse, which the guide ties to structured and semi-structured data.
notes.example: Like a reservoir fed by many streams: a research institute pours sensor readings, images and log files into one store to explore later.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data storage”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the data supply chain?
notes.back: The sequence of steps data passes through in an organisation, from its genesis to its activation.
notes.explanation: The study guide lists six steps in all; collection, processing, storage and analysis come between the first and the last.
notes.example: Like a food supply chain that runs from farm to plate: data too has a starting point, several handling steps and a point where it is finally used.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data supply chain”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is data governance?
notes.back: A framework of processes, roles and standards that ensures information is used effectively to achieve organisational goals.
notes.explanation: It is about rules as much as tools: the study guide says it sets who may access and manage data, and how and when.
notes.example: Like a library’s lending rules: who may borrow which books, for how long, and who is responsible for the rare collection.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data governance”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a data silo?
notes.back: Information trapped in an isolated system, cut off from other tools and systems.
notes.explanation: Google lists silos among the risks AI initiatives face without governance, because information trapped in isolated systems blocks a unified data lakehouse.
notes.example: Like a filing cabinet locked in one department’s office: sales figures that only the sales team’s system can reach.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is data governance?”, “Why modern data governance is critical for AI”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is vendor lock-in?
notes.back: Being locked into a single provider, such as one cloud provider.
notes.explanation: Google names multicloud as one way to avoid it, since it lets enterprises choose the best solution for their needs.
notes.example: Like a printer that takes only its maker’s ink: a firm whose data and apps are built around one provider’s proprietary tools.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Drivers, considerations, strategy, and approaches”, “Business and technical drivers”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Avoiding vendor lock-in: Sometimes, enterprises want to avoid being locked into a single cloud provider. A multicloud approach lets them choose the best solution for their business needs.

notes.front: What is Knowledge Catalog?
notes.back: A Gemini-powered context layer that provides business context and grounding across an organisation’s whole data estate.
notes.explanation: It builds a dynamic context graph from structured and unstructured data, helping teams discover assets and verify data quality.
notes.example: Like a library catalogue that also explains what each book is for: a retailer’s analysts search it to find which table holds online orders.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Knowledge Catalog overview”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Knowledge Catalog is a Gemini-powered context layer that provides universal business context and active grounding capabilities across your entire data estate. notes.front: According to the study guide, where does the importance of data lie?
notes.back: In its ability to power smarter, real-time decisions and personalised customer experiences.
notes.explanation: The guide describes data as raw information, structured and unstructured, that an organisation collects from every interaction and process.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “The value of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two reasons the exam guide gives for why data is valuable?
notes.back: Any two, among others: generating real-time business insights, identifying trends, and informing strategic decisions.
notes.explanation: The exam guide gives these as examples, so the list is open; it also names fuelling artificial intelligence.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader exam guide, Section 2, objective 2.1, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A coffee chain combines its till receipts, loyalty-app activity and online reviews, and notices that oat-milk orders are rising in one area weeks before its rivals do. Which value of data does this show?
notes.back: A: analysing varied data to spot trends early and stay competitive.
notes.choices:
A) Perceiving emerging trends to keep a competitive edge
B) Avoiding integration tax
C) Reducing network latency
D) Lowering bandwidth needs
notes.choicesExplained: B: integration tax is a driver of transformation, not something analysis of sales data delivers. C: latency is a network travel time. D: bandwidth is a network capacity, unrelated to what the data reveals.
notes.explanation: The study guide says analysing everything from financial reports to social media sentiment lets organisations perceive emerging trends, predict needs and keep a competitive edge.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “The value of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do a database, a data warehouse and a data lake differ?
notes.back: A database stores organised data in tables; a warehouse analyses structured and semi-structured data from many sources; a lake holds raw data of any type.
notes.explanation: Each meets a different need in the study guide: organised tables, analysis and reporting across sources, or raw data of any type and volume.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data storage”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A research institute wants one repository that can take in sensor readings, microscope images and raw log files in any volume, keep them in raw form and let scientists explore and process them later. Which fits?
notes.back: A: a lake ingests and stores any type or volume of raw data.
notes.choices:
A) A data lake
B) A data warehouse
C) A database
D) A data silo
notes.choicesExplained: B: a warehouse is for analysing structured and semi-structured data, not raw images. C: a database holds organised data in tables. D: a silo is trapped data, the opposite of a shared repository.
notes.explanation: The study guide defines a data lake as a repository to ingest, store, explore, process and analyse any type or volume of raw data, regardless of source.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data storage”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A supermarket group wants to bring together structured sales figures from the systems of all its regional divisions, so that head office can analyse them and produce company-wide reports. Which fits?
notes.back: C: an enterprise system for analysis and reporting on data from multiple sources.
notes.choices:
A) A data lake of raw files
B) A data silo
C) A data warehouse
D) Open source software
notes.choicesExplained: A: a lake is aimed at raw data of any type, while this is structured data gathered for reporting. B: a silo keeps data isolated, the opposite of the goal. D: open source describes how software is licensed, not a way to store data.
notes.explanation: The study guide describes a data warehouse as an enterprise system used for analysis and reporting of structured and semi-structured data from multiple sources.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data storage”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A dental practice needs to keep patient names, appointments and treatments in tables that its booking app reads and updates all day. Which fits?
notes.back: C: an organised collection of data in tables, accessed electronically.
notes.choices:
A) A data lake
B) A data silo
C) A database
D) A data warehouse
notes.choicesExplained: A: a lake is for raw data of any type in large volumes, not an app’s day-to-day records. B: a silo is a problem to avoid, not a store to choose. D: a warehouse is for analysis and reporting across multiple sources.
notes.explanation: One application’s organised records in tables are what the study guide’s definition of a database describes.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Data storage”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An online bookshop records which titles each customer browses and buys on its own website. What kind of data is this for the bookshop?
notes.back: C: collected directly by the business from its own customers.
notes.choices:
A) Third-party data
B) Second-party data
C) First-party data
D) Unstructured data only
notes.choicesExplained: A: third-party data comes from collectors with no direct customer relationship. B: second-party data is owned by another organisation such as a partner. D: browsing and purchase records can be neatly organised, and ‘party’ is about who collected the data, not its shape.
notes.explanation: First-party data is proprietary customer data a business gathers itself through its own transactions and digital interactions.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Types of data”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An airline receives booking data owned by its partner hotel chain and uses it to enrich its own customer records. What kind of data is the hotel’s booking data for the airline?
notes.back: C: another organisation’s data, from a partner, used to augment the airline’s own.
notes.choices:
A) First-party data
B) Third-party data
C) Second-party data
D) Structured data only
notes.choicesExplained: A: the airline did not collect it from its own customers. B: third-party data comes from collectors with no direct customer relationship, and the hotel has one. D: its shape is not what the question is about; ownership is.
notes.explanation: The study guide defines second-party data as data owned by another organisation, such as a partner, used to augment a company’s internal datasets.

A) First-party data
B) Semi-structured data only
C) Second-party data
